cells.tense: The back-and-forth has settled into something you stand on — what you give and what comes back are one motion now, and the motion is what you're made of.
cells.ask: Say thank you out loud today to one person for one specific thing they did this week. Not a text — the voice, with the thing named.
cells.core:
Someone does something for you and you give back. No ledger needed; the return arrives in kind and it arrives on time. That's the settled version of this — doing good by people and letting them do good by you without either side checking the balance after.

It shows up in small ways. You remember what they did. You give back unhurried, without a price tag attached for next time. What's left is making the return audible once: today, say thank you out loud to one person and name the thing they did. What that does is let them hear it, instead of you assuming it landed because you felt it.
cells.sheetLine: You give back, and you don't attach a price to it.
cells.verb: give back in kind, out loud, where it can be seen
cells.place: the ground where a person becomes what they actually are

cells.tense: You're already checking the balance of something that hasn't happened — running numbers on a return nobody asked for, on an exchange that isn't due yet.
cells.ask: Do one thing for someone today without tallying it afterward. No pause to work out what it cost you or what it earns you.
cells.core:
A friend does something kind and before you've said thank you, the arithmetic is done — what you owe, how soon, in what form. The math is quick and it's correct, and it's also happening before the exchange has actually taken place. The calmer version is the one where fairness moves with the moment rather than ahead of it: kindness lands, you answer it, and the answer isn't priced in advance.

Today, do something for one person without tallying it afterward. Don't decide what it earns you or what you'll owe them next time. If it helps, picture a camera watching: you hand them the thing, you say one sentence, you walk away. The point isn't calm. The point is one exchange that finishes without your hand on the scale.
cells.sheetLine: You've priced the exchange before it was offered.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that's already behind you — somebody gave you something and you didn't put your answer back into the world, and the exchange is still open because of it.
cells.ask: Message one person today and ask them for one specific thing you actually want from them this week. Not a general offer to help — a real request with a name attached.
cells.core:
Give the other person something good and you'll do it well — that direction is available to you. It's the other one that got put down: someone extended a hand and the answer went unwritten, and the moment passed while you were deciding what the return should be. That's the part with slack in it, and it doesn't need a story to work on.

This week, message one person and ask them for one specific thing you want. Not 'let me know if you ever need anything' — an actual request. It might feel too big to make. That discomfort is the usable part: the line doesn't get found by staying on the side of it you know.
cells.sheetLine: You give, and you don't let it come back.

cells.tense: Something in you keeps track of what's owed and to whom, and the way you tell it, that tracking is just what happens in the room — not something you're doing.
cells.ask: Write two lines today: one thing you did for someone this week that nobody saw, and one thing someone did that you haven't acknowledged. Read them back once.
cells.core:
Somebody mentions a friend and the ledger appears: who paid for lunch last, whose turn it is to reach out. In how you describe it, that's just how any group works — 'anyone would have noticed.' The looking, though, is yours, and it runs in the background without ever being said in your own voice.

Pushing harder at the invisible version doesn't get you anywhere, because there's nothing to push on. What works is making it visible in the smallest way. Two lines, today: one thing you did for someone this week that nobody saw, and one thing someone did that you haven't said out loud. Reading it back is the first time you hear the fairness you carry in your own voice.

attempts.check: The one personal claim I can't support is any word about what the person has actually been doing — the record says only that fairness is exchanged with others and that the seat is becoming what they are, so the cells must locate the condition in a moment ('when someone does something for you', 'something you did quietly for years') rather than assert the fact of their behaviour. A reader could fairly say 'I am already the one who gives back' — which is why the Balanced cell says the returning is what makes the self the self, not that the person invented it, and why the Too Little cell leaves the door unsolved rather than naming what happened behind it. The asks survive a wrong read: if the accounting isn't actually running, writing down one gift given and one received still teaches something about where the receipts come from, and asking one specific person for one specific thing still works whether or not pride is the reason it hasn't been asked. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is any 'what's coming is yours already' phrasing — it sounds like a benediction and gives the person nothing to do, so I've put the move in the ending of the Balanced tense line instead, as recognition rather than an announcement.
